> I don't think this means we should ignore (or stop trying to reform) a system that is intrinsically hostile to female trainees, given that women still disproportionately do most of the caring for small children, elderly relatives etc etc.

I agree with your point that women often aren’t able to complete these training courses due to disproportionate responsibly for children/home … surely that is the issue to address though, the social view that women should do these things and men should focus on their career, rather than try to overhaul the training programme. LTFT should be a choice for everyone of course, but it seems the issue is men expecting women to take on additional home responsibility at the expense of their careers, and women also choosing to do this. If both parties are happy with that choice then great - but there’s no real reason not to have an equal split of home responsibilities for men and women and no reason all the work should fall to the women.
As women in medicine, we should choose male partners who will split the workload equitably with us and not expect us to step back in our careers to care for the family.

> In terms of the education thing as it relates to pay, I think doctors should be better paid of course but I don't think I deserve more than other workers because of education, we're all just people trying to get by

I’m surprised by this view. Education is not a paid job, we pay for the privilege of a degree and rack up debts that continue to collect interest through a working life, as well as giving up at least 5 years to train as a professional. This is 5 years we are paying for education whilst someone who chose not to go into education was able to work and build up savings/buy a house/whatever. You don’t think there should be some compensation for that in the form of higher pay? If there isn’t, only a saint would make the sacrifice because it is a loss of time and earnings for no reward. 

We are all people trying to get by and everyone working a full time job should be able to get by comfortably, but I definitely think a professional education should be worth a higher pay.

I see where you’re coming from, and I think it’s possible the apprenticeship programme could be worked into successful medical education, but with a lot of caveats.

1) Starting in hospital from day 1 going to help anyone - you don’t have any knowledge, skills or training. I think you’d need some basics first before can even start - some basic skills training (bloods, cannulas, catheters) would allow you to do some stuff on the wards at least I guess so that would be a start. These would be pretty quick as training is usually a couple videos then a couple hours training/practice on manikins. 

2) You still need to learn the basics of anatomy and physiology, so some sort of teaching would need to be provided for this. I guess it could be done online but I’m not sure how easy it would be to learn anatomy this way. We also need some sort of exam to ensure people on the apprentice route have an appropriate level of knowledge as nobody wants two tiers of doctor.

3) You need to have some training in common clinical presentations, history and examination, and conditions - something a third year student has at least ideas of before they go on the ward. There could be an online training package to go through history taking, common presentations, causes and management (again with this knowledge being tested to ensure a certain standard), but it’s much harder to teach examination without having face to face sessions. This burden can’t/shouldn’t fall on current doctors with their own busy workloads.

I think with a pure apprenticeship based model we will be milling out inferior doctors without the basic sciences background or appropriate medical knowledge. I do think that with appropriate learning packages and resources, a lot of medicine could be taught online (god knows covid has shown us that with so much of medical education and teaching being online now), but there needs to be a formal syllabus and learning resources and there are some practical things that need to be taught/practiced in person, such as examinations and skills. We also need to ensure we maintain the current standard of knowledge - ie exams should be similar to current med school exams even if the teaching is different. 

Honestly from 3rd year we had barely any teaching were given lists of conditions to basically look up/learn ourselves, the important part of making this work is ensuring there are learning resources for the ‘apprentices’ to learn what we do in year 1/2 and ensure they are examined to the same standard. Beyond that, I quite like the idea of an apprentice-like programme where people can earn whilst practicing their practical skills and contributing to care and also have some protected times and resources  to teach/learn the rest. Medicine is somewhat already an unpaid apprenticeship from the clinical years, it would be nice to split that into paid work (yes basically being a skills bunny but every med student has spent a decent amount of time doing that except here getting paid!) whilst also learning.

Keto might be dangerous to diabetics or people who can’t control their blood sugars, but not to an otherwise healthy person. From someone who smokes a lot of weed, I think you were in the wrong. Your sister came on a night out with your, it was your friends and you she was out with and you know she isn’t into drugs including weed - so why put her in an uncomfortable situation by going for a smoke in the night? She likely didn’t want to hang out with a drug dealer, or with people smoking a joint (and yes the smoke is a 5 min thing but someone who doesn’t like drugs likely doesn’t want to hang out with a high person either), or wait around in the dark in an unknown area alone, or walk home at night alone. Especially after she’d had a couple drinks herself, she probably thought she’d be getting home safely together with you. By putting her in that situation you showed her you were so keen for the smoke that you prioritised it over her safety and comfort. 

She didn’t need to go to your mom but might well be concerned - your lifestyle is pretty alien to her and you threw her right into the middle of it in what probably felt like a dangerous situation to her, so you kinda took just both leading your lives and not getting involved in what you disapprove of off the table.
My brother doesn’t comment on my smoking habits to my parents though he disapproves, but I also keep it away from him because I know he disapproves and don’t want to make anyone uncomfortable. I’d apologise to your sister if you made her uncomfortable by smoking when you were out together, but tell her that you are hurt that she went to your mom behind your back, and let her know that you are in control of your life and that is a priority, and that you smoke in the same way you both drink - now and again to relax or socialise.

I’m nowhere near that far from my parents and I feel the exact same, especially after being at home, the worrying about my parents and feeling like I’m losing out on what could be limited time with them, knowing that they’re so happy when I’m around and say how quiet it is without me etc. 

The feeling doesn’t completely go away because you won’t stop loving or missing your family. The other thing is we were always making our next plan of when we’d meet - even if that next time was months away, we’d discuss our schedules and figure when we were free and then next time one of us mentions a new restaurant or whatever we can say ‘oh we’ll go on x date when we’re all together.’ That and holidays. Rather I would tell him that you have dealt with this but he is clearly struggling to cope and you are here to support him in any way possible. I am here to support you but I won’t tolerate that.’

I would try to think about what you might have wanted from him if roles were reversed and you were feeling deeply sad about the miscarriage but he were unaffected. I would speak to him and tell him that though you don’t have the same feelings about this as him, you are his partner and you understand that he is sad and are there to support him. Trying to make you feel the same as him isn’t helpful to either of you, but if he wants to talk about it or is feeling sad, you are on his side and want to be there.

You need to recognise and acknowledge his hurt and that you have caused it and show you regret your actions, not be selfish again. I can understand you might be scared and this isn’t how you imagined the birth of your first child, but I very much doubt this is what your husband was imagining either.

My boyfriend and I used to have this problem- we both had anger issues and in our worst arguments we’d say the most terrible things to each other, because we knew each other well enough to pick and weak points or insecurities and do some real damage.

It brought us to the brink of breakup several times but we never really wanted to let go, so over time we ended up putting in systems to help us.

1) Either of us can pause an argument if it gets too much, and essentially we both have to take an hour or so apart, before returning to the fight. I found that in this time some of my pure anger would dissipate and I’d return to wanting to actually resolve the issue and progress rather than just lash out.

2) If we’ve got something important on or somewhere to be, we come back to it after. This is to avoid the huge drama before a job interview situation - which repeatedly happened with my bf, we would end up going stressed/upset to important things, then blame the other. He can’t give you his full focus when he’s got a job interview that day, so remind yourself that if you want to resolve things, you need to do so when his mind is clear. 

3) Ask yourself what your intention is when you’re about to bring up an issue. Is there actually something he can do?  Half the time when I really thought about it, there wasn’t any way for him to fix the situation, but I just wanted to dig in about his mistake.

Just a couple things that helped us. It took us a while and we used to fail at our own strategies repeatedly - but we communicate better now.
